steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on out-of-distribution detection for text generators, where we introduce the LOFTER benchmark and the RAINPROOF detector. Explain why deployed generators face distribution shift, why classification-style OOD methods don't carry over easily, the constraints we work under, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Text generators, the closed-world assumption and distribution shift
2. OOD detection so far and why text generation is harder
3. Our goal and four constraints
4. Contributions: LOFTER, RAINPROOF, insights, code

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Text generators and distribution shift
- progress in NLG: generic (GPT, LLAMA and variants) and task-specific (Grover, Pegasus, DialogGPT) generators
- power public MT systems and chatbots; reliability prerequisite for adoption
- trained in closed world: train/test i.i.d. from one distribution (in-distribution)
- deployed in open world; i.i.d. often violated; shifts reduce performance
- need tools against harmful shifts; unresolved practical problem
- examples: translation model on another language (Spanish model on Catalan, Dutch model on Afrikaans) or unexpected technical language (colloquial model, rare medical terms)
- released behind API -> rules out many features-based OOD methods

2. OOD detection
- most work on classification; (conditional) text generation mainly unexplored though highly exposed
- training-aware methods: expose network to OOD samples during training
- plug-in methods: separate IN from OOD by model behaviour on new input; MSP, Energy, feature-based anomaly detectors with per-class scores
- adapting to text generation harder: sequence of classification problems (next token) but vocabulary two orders of magnitude larger

3. Goal and constraints
- new tools for more reliable text generators in practical systems
- 4 constraints: (i) no access to OOD samples; (ii) black-box: only soft probability outputs, no internal states; (iii) easy to use on top of any model; (iv) filter OOD samples and also improve average end-task performance

4. Contributions
1. LOFTER benchmark (Language Out oF disTribution pErformance benchmaRk)
- existing work: English only, GLUE, OOD detection performance only
- realistic generative shifts beyond English: close language pairs (Spanish/Catalan, Dutch/Afrikaans), domain change (medical vs news vs dialogs)
- detectors evaluated jointly with system's end-task performance
2. RAINPROOF detector (Relative informAItioN Projection Out OF distribution detector)
- fully unsupervised; works without reference IN samples (\mathbb{s}_{0}) and with them (\mathbb{s}_{1})
- \mathbb{s}_{0}: negentropy of predictions as normality measure; \mathbb{s}_{1}: Information Projection with reference set
3. Insights on operational value
- detectors may drop well-processed (well translated) samples and keep bad ones -> weaker performance
- RAINPROOF improves end-task performance while removing most OOD samples
4. Code: plug-and-play library on top of Transformers, detectors and baselines

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In recent years there has been significant progress in Natural Language Generation (NLG), with powerful generic text generators (e.g., GPT, LLAMA and its variants) and task-specific ones (e.g., Grover, Pegasus and DialogGPT). They power machine translation (MT) systems or chatbots that the public uses, and they need to be reliable to be adopted. Text generators are trained in a so-called closed world, where the training and test data are assumed to be drawn i.i.d. from a single distribution, called the in-distribution. But when they are deployed, these models work in an open world where the i.i.d. assumption is often violated. Changes in the data distribution are harmful and cause a drop in performance. We need tools that protect models from harmful distribution shifts, because this is clearly an unresolved practical problem. For example, a trained translation model should not be expected to be reliable when it gets another language (e.g. a Spanish model getting Catalan, or a Dutch model getting Afrikaans) or unexpected technical language (e.g., a colloquial translation model getting rare technical terms from the medical field). These models also tend to be released behind an API, and this rules out many of the usual features-based OOD detection methods.

Most work on Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) detection is about classification, so OOD detection in (conditional) text generation is mostly unexplored, even though text generation is among the most exposed applications. Existing solutions are in two categories. The first one, training-aware methods, changes the classifier training by exposing the neural network to OOD samples during training. The second one, plug-in methods, tries to distinguish regular samples in the in-distribution (IN) from OOD samples based on how the model behaves on a new input. Plug-in methods include Maximum Softmax Probabilities (MSP) or Energy or feature-based anomaly detectors that compute an anomaly score per class. Plug-in methods from classification look attractive, but adapting them to text generation tasks is more involved. Text generation can be seen as a sequence of classification problems, i.e., choosing the next token at each step, but the number of possible tokens is two orders of magnitude higher than in usual classification setups.

3. Goal and constraints
- new tools for more reliable text generators in practical systems
- 4 constraints: (i) no access to OOD samples; (ii) black-box: only soft probability outputs, no internal states; (iii) easy to use on top of any model; (iv) filter OOD samples and also improve average end-task performance

4. Contributions
1. LOFTER benchmark (Language Out oF disTribution pErformance benchmaRk)
- existing work: English only, GLUE, OOD detection performance only
- realistic generative shifts beyond English: close language pairs (Spanish/Catalan, Dutch/Afrikaans), domain change (medical vs news vs dialogs)
- detectors evaluated jointly with system's end-task performance
2. RAINPROOF detector (Relative informAItioN Projection Out OF distribution detector)
- fully unsupervised; works without reference IN samples (\mathbb{s}_{0}) and with them (\mathbb{s}_{1})
- \mathbb{s}_{0}: negentropy of predictions as normality measure; \mathbb{s}_{1}: Information Projection with reference set
3. Insights on operational value
- detectors may drop well-processed (well translated) samples and keep bad ones -> weaker performance
- RAINPROOF improves end-task performance while removing most OOD samples
4. Code: plug-and-play library on top of Transformers, detectors and baselines

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In recent years there has been significant progress in Natural Language Generation (NLG), with powerful generic text generators (e.g., GPT, LLAMA and its variants) and task-specific ones (e.g., Grover, Pegasus and DialogGPT). They power machine translation (MT) systems or chatbots that the public uses, and they need to be reliable to be adopted. Text generators are trained in a so-called closed world, where the training and test data are assumed to be drawn i.i.d. from a single distribution, called the in-distribution. But when they are deployed, these models work in an open world where the i.i.d. assumption is often violated. Changes in the data distribution are harmful and cause a drop in performance. We need tools that protect models from harmful distribution shifts, because this is clearly an unresolved practical problem. For example, a trained translation model should not be expected to be reliable when it gets another language (e.g. a Spanish model getting Catalan, or a Dutch model getting Afrikaans) or unexpected technical language (e.g., a colloquial translation model getting rare technical terms from the medical field). These models also tend to be released behind an API, and this rules out many of the usual features-based OOD detection methods.

Most work on Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) detection is about classification, so OOD detection in (conditional) text generation is mostly unexplored, even though text generation is among the most exposed applications. Existing solutions are in two categories. The first one, training-aware methods, changes the classifier training by exposing the neural network to OOD samples during training. The second one, plug-in methods, tries to distinguish regular samples in the in-distribution (IN) from OOD samples based on how the model behaves on a new input. Plug-in methods include Maximum Softmax Probabilities (MSP) or Energy or feature-based anomaly detectors that compute an anomaly score per class. Plug-in methods from classification look attractive, but adapting them to text generation tasks is more involved. Text generation can be seen as a sequence of classification problems, i.e., choosing the next token at each step, but the number of possible tokens is two orders of magnitude higher than in usual classification setups.

In this work our goal is to develop new tools to build more reliable text generators that can be used in practical systems. We work under 4 constraints: (i) We do not assume access to OOD samples; (ii) We are in a black-box scenario: we do not assume access to the internal states of the model, only to the soft probability distributions it outputs; (iii) The detectors should be easy to use on top of any existing model, so they are adaptable; (iv) OOD detectors should not only filter OOD samples, they should also improve the average performance on the end-task of the model.

Our contributions. Our main contributions are:

1. A more operational benchmark for OOD detection in text generation. We present LOFTER, the Language Out oF disTribution pErformance benchmaRk. Existing works on OOD detection for language modelling focus on (i) only the English language, (ii) the GLUE benchmark, and (iii) measure performance only in terms of OOD detection. LOFTER introduces more realistic data shifts in the generative setting that go beyond English: language shifts from closely related language pairs (e.g., Spanish and Catalan or Dutch and Afrikaans) and domain change (e.g., medical vs news data or vs dialogs). LOFTER also has an updated evaluation setting, where the performance of the detectors is evaluated together with the overall system's performance on the end task.

2. A new detector inspired by information projection. We present RAINPROOF, a Relative informAItioN Projection Out OF distribution detector. RAINPROOF is fully unsupervised. It is flexible and can be used both when no reference samples (IN) are available (scenario \mathbb{s}_{0}) and when they are (scenario \mathbb{s}_{1}). For \mathbb{s}_{0}, RAINPROOF computes the negentropy of the model's predictions and uses it as a measure of normality. For \mathbb{s}_{1}, it uses the natural extension of this: the Information Projection, which uses a reference set to get a data-driven notion of normality.

3. New insights on the operational value of OOD detectors. Our experiments on LOFTER show that OOD detectors can filter out samples that the model processes well (i.e. translates well) and keep samples that it does not, which leads to weaker performance. Our results show that RAINPROOF improves the performance on the end task while removing most of the OOD samples.

4. Code and reproducibility. We release a plug-and-play library built on the Transformers library that implements our detectors and the baselines.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Significant progress has been made in Natural Language Generation (NLG) in recent years, with the development of powerful generic (e.g., GPT [1,2,3], LLAMA [4] and its variants) and task-specific (e.g., Grover [5], Pegasus [6] and DialogGPT [7]) text generators. They power machine translation (MT) systems or chatbots that are exposed to the public, and their reliability is a prerequisite for adoption. Text generators are trained in the context of a so-called closed world [8], where training and test data are assumed to be drawn i.i.d. from a single distribution, known as the in-distribution. However, once deployed, these models operate in an open world [9,10] where the i.i.d. assumption is often violated. Changes in data distribution are detrimental and induce a drop in performance. It is necessary to develop tools to protect models from harmful distribution shifts, as this is a clearly unresolved practical problem [11]. For example, a trained translation model is not expected to be reliable when presented with another language (e.g. a Spanish model exposed to Catalan, or a Dutch model exposed to Afrikaans) or with unexpected technical language (e.g., a colloquial translation model exposed to rare technical terms from the medical field). Such models also tend to be released behind an API [12], which rules out many usual features-based OOD detection methods.

Most work on Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) detection focuses on classification, leaving OOD detection in (conditional) text generation settings mainly unexplored, even though it is among the most exposed applications. Existing solutions fall into two categories. The first, called training-aware methods [13,14,15], modifies the classifier training by exposing the neural network to OOD samples during training. The second, called plug-in methods, aims to distinguish regular samples in the in-distribution (IN) from OOD samples based on the model's behaviour on a new input. Plug-in methods include Maximum Softmax Probabilities (MSP) [16] or Energy [17] or feature-based anomaly detectors that compute a per-class anomaly score [18,19,20,21]. Although plug-in methods from classification settings seem attractive, adapting them to text generation tasks is more involved: while text generation can be seen as a sequence of classification problems, i.e., choosing the next token at each step, the number of possible tokens is two orders of magnitude higher than in usual classification setups.

In this work, we aim to develop new tools to build more reliable text generators that can be used in practical systems. To do so, we work under 4 constraints: (i) We do not assume access to OOD samples; (ii) We suppose a black-box scenario: we do not assume access to the internal states of the model but only to the soft probability distributions it outputs; (iii) The detectors should be easy to use on top of any existing model to ensure adaptability; (iv) OOD detectors should not only filter OOD samples but also improve the average performance on the end-task the model has to perform.

Our contributions. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

1. A more operational benchmark for text generation OOD detection. We present LOFTER, the Language Out oF disTribution pErformance benchmaRk. Existing works on OOD detection for language modelling [11] focus on (i) the English language only, (ii) the GLUE benchmark, and (iii) measure performance solely in terms of OOD detection. LOFTER introduces more realistic data shifts in the generative setting that go beyond English: language shifts induced by closely related language pairs (e.g., Spanish and Catalan or Dutch and Afrikaans [22]) and domain change (e.g., medical vs news data or vs dialogs). In addition, LOFTER comes with an updated evaluation setting in which detectors' performance is jointly evaluated w.r.t. the overall system's performance on the end task.

2. A novel detector inspired by information projection. We present RAINPROOF, a Relative informAItioN Projection Out OF distribution detector. RAINPROOF is fully unsupervised. It is flexible and can be applied both when no reference samples (IN) are available (scenario \mathbb{s}_{0}) and when they are (scenario \mathbb{s}_{1}). RAINPROOF tackles \mathbb{s}_{0} by computing the negentropy [23] of the model's predictions and using it as a measure of normality. For \mathbb{s}_{1}, it relies on its natural extension, the Information Projection [24], which uses a reference set to get a data-driven notion of normality.

3. New insights on the operational value of OOD detectors. Our experiments on LOFTER show that OOD detectors may filter out samples that are well processed (i.e. well translated) by the model and keep samples that are not, leading to weaker performance. Our results show that RAINPROOF improves performance on the end task while removing most of the OOD samples.

4. Code and reproducibility. We release a plug-and-play library built upon the Transformers library that implements our detectors and baselines.
